Advertisement for the post of JRF in a NTTM funded Research Project Applications are invited from suitable candidates for Junior Research Fellow (JRF) to work on the research project sponsored by National Technical Textile Mission, Ministry of Textile (7/MSG/NTTM- 2023/7th MSG/8), under the supervision of Dr. Mukesh Bajya (PI), Department of Textile Technology, NIT Jalandhar Title of the project: Development of cost-effective ballistic and stab resistance soft body armour by using different high performance materials Duration of the project: 2 years Appointment will be ON PURELY TEMPORARY BASIS, for a maximum period of two years or project durations whichever is earlier based on the performance. Project position and Number: JRF (02) Fellowship amount: Rs. 37,000/- + HRA as per institute/project norms. Eligibility requirements: Post graduate degree in basic science (Physics and chemistry) with NET qualification or Graduate in Textile Technology/ Textile Engineering with GATE or M.Tech in Textiles/ Polymer/ Fiber Science / Chemical Engineering / Material Science / Chemistry / Physics / Mechanical / Paper and Pulp /Nanotechnology/relevant branches.

LUMINESCENCE RESEARCH ARTICLE Thermoluminescence dosimeter (TLD) studies of Ca;9K(PO,4)7:Dy phosphor for applications in radiation dosimetry Sansar Chand, Rohit Mehra ga Vibha Chopra First published: 25 July 2023 | https://doi.org/10.1002/bic.4564 PDF A TOOLS «@ SHARE Abstract This paper reports the thermoluminescence (TL) aspects of Ca;gK(PO.)7:Dy phosphor synthesized by the wet chemical method for the first time. The XRD results confirm the formation of the desired crystalline phase. Surface morphological studies reveal the formation of polyhedrons and agglomerations having an average diameter of 200 nm while EDS data shows the presence and composition of the elements in appropriate amounts. The effect of Dy doping concentration has been studied on the thermoluminescence properties with exposure to gamma radiations from the Co-60 source. Best TL has been observed for 5 mol% Dy doping concentration. The glow curve is simple and consists of a single peak at 130°C. The effect of the heating rate has been studied on the TL glow curve and the heating rate of 5°C/s shows the best TL response.

RTPESES-2023
ABOUT THE SHORT-TERM COURSE The importance of power electronics has grown over the years due to several factors. Power electronics is interdisciplinary in nature, and it is used in a wide variety of applications like electric drives, power quality in power systems and renewable energy systems, etc... Therefore, an STC on “Recent Trends in Power Electronics and Sustainable Energy Systems (RTPESES-2023)” would be an exciting course to attend as it directly belongs to an emerging area of research. Therefore, the key focus of the STC should include but not be limited to the following topics: (a) applications of machine learning in electrical engineering, (b) design of new DC-DC converters with fault-tolerant capabilities for renewable energy systems, (c) modern control techniques in electric vehicle technologies, and (d) application of power electronics in renewable energy systems, (e) control and protection of wise and microgrids. TOPICS TO BE COVERED ❖ Applications of Machine Learning in Electrical Engineering ❖ Design of new DC-DC Converters for Renewable Energy Systems with Fault Tolerant Capabilities

The department has unique research facilities that enable leading-edge research in many areas such as Robotics and Automation, Process Control, Biomedical Instrumentation, Sensors and Wireless Networking and Intelligent Control Systems. These facilities provide an excellent opportunity for graduate students and research scholars to be trained and gain valuable experience. The Department is consolidating its efforts to promote industrial research and consultancy in relevant areas. For other reputed Institute(s), NIT Jalandhar should have MoUs with such Institutes/Organizations. | NY hear Siow re 45 on ECPC-405 Advanced Mobile Communications [3 0.0 3] Course Objectives This course provides a comprehensive overview of mobile communications, covering the evolution from 1G to 5G. Students will gain an understanding of analog and digital systems, voice and messaging services, GSM, CDMA, and advancements like GPRS, EDGE, UMTS, and HSPA. The course also explores 4G LTE, LTE Advanced Pro, VoLTE, OFDM, MIMO, and introduces the potential and applications of 5G. Students will learn about SG network components, including NR, NOMA, massive MIMO, network slicing, and SDN. The course addresses 5G deployment, challenges, spectrum access, rural connectivity, and emerging technologies such as LEOs and HAP/UAV. Course Content Mobile Communications Overview: Evolution from 1G to 5G, Analog voice systems in 1G, digital radio systems in 2G, voice and messaging services, TDMA based GSM, CDMA, 2.5G (GPRS), 2.75G (EDGE); IMT2000, 3G UMTS, W-CDMA, HSPA, HSPA+, 3G services and data rates, IMT Advanced, 4G, LTE, VoLTE, OFDM, MIMO, LTE Advanced Pro (3GPP Release 13+), IMT2020, enhancements in

AMBEDKAR NATIONAL INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY JALANDHAR DEPARTMENT OF ELECTRICAL ENGINEERING 16-20 February 2024 About the Course: As the world is shifting towards renewables, power industry is experiencing a fundamental change in its operation. Witnessing the advantages of digital technology in other industries, there is a need of digital reinvention in power industry also. Digital Grid, integrating technologies in embedded sensing, advanced intelligence, data analytics and cloud computing, leverages customer-sited distributed energy resources to enhance grid flexibility. Digital twin technology, a vital part of digital grid, uses simulation, machine learning and reasoning along with real-time data to provide valuable insights regarding the equipment and the processes. Digital grid is envisioned to achieve a robust wide-area grid through controlled flow of energy. Digital technologies bring together distributed energy sources, electric vehicle, and energy storage devices to create smarter, greener cities, buildings, and homes. The idea of digital grid is based on utilizing the abundant energy available from renewable resources. Realisation of digital grid
title: DGTSEF1.3

text:
DGTSEF1.3
digital grid is based on utilizing the abundant energy available from renewable resources. Realisation of digital grid involves the need to establish strong regulatory and cyber security protocols to be built in the network. This short- term course is designed to prepare the future workforce for a high-data world, ensuring they have the technical knowledge necessary to be actively involved in the realization of digital grid. se will gain insights into the concept of digital grid, challenges in transforming power grid to digital grid and enabling technologies and data platforms to realize the Digital Grid vision. They will also learn about latest advances, emerging policies, and breakthrough re- search on customer DER integration. Advertisement for the post of Junior Research Fellow (JRF) Applications are invited from eligible candidates for one temporary post of Junior Research Fellow (JRF) in the SERB-DST (EMEQ) funded research project (EEQ/2023/000511) entitled, “Smart Wettability Surfaces Instigating Spontaneous Autonomous Contact Line Motion for Droplet Based Sensing and Self-Cleaning Surfaces” undertaken in the Department of Chemistry, NIT Jalandhar. Understanding the relationship between entrepreneurship education, entrepreneurial attitudes, and entrepreneurial intentions among engineering graduates: the moderating role of gender Manpreet Kaur and Sonia Chawla Department of Humanities and Management, Dr BR Ambedkar National Institute of Technology, Jalandhar, India Abstract Purpose – The current study assesses the contribution of entrepreneurship education (EE) in strengthening entrepreneurial attitudes (EAs) and entrepreneurial intentions (EIs) among engineering graduates in India. Design/methodology/approach – Cross-sectional data were collected through an electronic questionnaire from 340 engineering students. Structural equation modeling was performed for hypothesis testing through SmartPLS4 software. Findings – The findings demonstrated that EE, EA and EI are positively and significantly correlated. However, the moderation effect of gender on EE–EI linkage was found to be insignificant. Research limitations/implications – The study provides comprehensive insights to understand EE effectiveness on students’ EI and further opens the path for future researchers to investigate how the inclusion of other constructs in theory of planned behavior and human capital theory can raise the EI among students.

Future research should target a larger sample size comprising students from diverse educational streams. Practical implications – The findings of this research offer various practical contributions for educational establishments, policymakers and the government in formulating constructive educational interventions that fully trigger the student’s EIs. Originality/value – This study adds to the scarce theoretical examination of EE–EI using the human capital approach in developing countries. In addition, this study is highly relevant to the scarce theoretical and empirical support for investigating the contribution of EE in HEIs in India. Introduction Entrepreneurs have invariably been acknowledged as the backbone of society for their enormous efforts to augment the standard of living embraced with innovativeness (Nowinski et al., 2019; Ratten and Jones, 2020; Sergi et al., 2019). In view of this, entrepreneurship education (EE) has now become the crucial educational intervention (Sanchez, 2013; Walter and Block, 2016), resulting in a radical growth in EE programs across HEIs along with an increase in scholarly work on the outcomes of EE (Bischoff et al., 2018; Hoang et al., 2021). EE enhances an individual’s stock of knowledge, skills and competencies, thereby raising the entrepreneurial attitudes (EAs) and entrepreneurial intentions (EIs) among university graduates (Carpenter and

individual’s stock of knowledge, skills and competencies, thereby raising the entrepreneurial attitudes (EAs) and entrepreneurial intentions (EIs) among university graduates (Carpenter and Wilson, 2022; Uddin et al., 2022). It has also been asserted that a knowledge base is crucial to develop the entrepreneurial potential of an individual, and thus, EE can create more and more able entrepreneurs (Katz, 2007; Pittaway and Cope, 2007). Numerous studies have advocated a positive and significant EE–EI association (Pisoni, 2019; Saptono et al., 2020), while others found a negative linkage (Oosterbeek et al., 2010) and others reported no association (Huber et al., 2014; Varamaki et al., 2015). These divergent outcomes showed significant gaps in the literature, which motivated the present study. Owing to the dynamic and interdisciplinary nature of EE, the field is still emerging and needs more inquiry (Ratten and Jones, 2020). EE context differs due to geographical, regional and cultural differences across nations worldwide, and consequently, the country’s entrepreneurial activities and outcomes vary due

Thus, it calls for more exploration into socioeconomic development resulting from EE–EI association in developing economies such as the Philippines, India, Peru, Argentina, etc. (Morris et al., 2020; Santos et al., 2019). Thus, theoretical evidence provides much support to investigate the problem in the Indian context along with the fact that the infusion of EE into university education is relatively a young phenomenon in Indian HEIs (Chhabra et al., 2021; Mukesh et al., 2018). Statistics also support that India has the most favorable entrepreneurial ecosystem among developing economies along with a substantial increase in total early stage entrepreneurial activity from 5.30% in 2020-2021 to 14.4% in 2021-22 (Global Entrepreneurship Monitor India Report 2021/22, 2022). Hence, HEIs hold an immense role in sustaining a favorable entrepreneurial context by providing an inclusive entrepreneurial

Hence, to address the gap and strengthen the literature on EE–EI relationship, the present study provides an inclusive framework that is grounded in the human capital theory (HCT) (Becker, 1964) and theory of planned behavior (TPB) (Ajzen, 1991). While gauging the literature, it was found that EE has got substantial recognition as a pathway to endorse attitudes, mindsets and intentions using the TPB framework (Cassol et al., 2022; Duong, 2022). The human capital approach of entrepreneurship, which is under searched area in EE literature especially in developing countries, is based on the belief that skills, knowledge and competencies make an individual efficient in starting and managing a business (Fayolle et al., 2006). Given this, EE is regarded as the most pervasive component of entrepreneurship

Given this, EE is regarded as the most pervasive component of entrepreneurship specific human capital investment (Unger et al., 2011; Martin et al., 2013). In addition, entrepreneurship is a planned activity that needs some kind of attitudinal preparation or mindset towards entrepreneurship, considering it the most robust dimension of TPB (Arshad et al., 2016; Kautonen et al., 2013). Against this backdrop, the current study investigated the effect of two exogenous variables, i.e. EE and EA, on EIs. The selection of these exogenous variables endorses the casual connection considering EE as a starting point that transforms EA, which eventually leads to EI formation. Furthermore, studies articulated that EI among males and females may be different (Pelegrini and Moraes, 2022; Taneja et al., 2023). Considering the gender-wise perspective, this study also explores how gender moderates EE–EI linkage. Human capital associated with entrepreneurship influences various stages of the entrepreneurial journey, such as opportunity recognition, business creation and business success (Marvel et al., 2016). Researchers affirm that individuals with solid cognitive aptitude can perform entrepreneurial activities more efficiently than individuals with weak cognitive abilities (Schenkel et al., 2012). Education and its interventions constitute an essential element of human capital formation and are certainly a significant path for acquiring new competencies and knowledge (Martin et al., 2013). It is noted that TPB concentrates on personality attributes such as attitude, self-efficacy and subjective norms as the potential predictors of EI (Krueger et al., 2000), where the human capital approach was used to comprehend entrepreneurship where people deliberately allot their resources as a response to dynamic economic situations (Schultz, 1980), implying that entrepreneurial potential can be raised through human capital. 2.2 Hypothesis formulation 2.2.1 Entrepreneurial education and entrepreneurial intentions. EE refers to the process of developing theoretical foundations, skills and competencies to recognize opportunities that others are unable to notice (Mwasalwiba, 2010). A plethora of studies have reported EE as a mechanism to stimulate an individual’s intention to start their own venture and promote economic development and business ventures (Nabi et al., 2018; Sherkat and Chenari, 2020). EE programs help to reinforce mindsets, attributes and business competencies in students (Bae et al., 2014; Nabi and Holden, 2008). Studies revealed that individuals who have gone through any EE program are better inclined toward venture creation than those who not have gone through any entrepreneurship course (Fitri Ayuni, 2018; Wardana et al., 2020). Concurrently, the study exhibited negative findings indicating that the acquisition of formal education decreases the probability of the creation of new establishments (Abdullahi et al., 2017). In addition, the linkage between EE and EI was verified based on entrepreneurial HCT (Saptono et al., 2020). According to HCT, education forms a part of intellectual capital that significantly influences the EI of an individual (Jogaratnam, 2017). In addition, limited studies exist in the Indian context that advocate the linkage between these two constructs (Biswas and Verma, 2022; Rajan and Panicker, 2020). Education offered by academic institutions cultivates students’ attitudes, which eventually affect their career decisions. Considering the socio- cultural context, EI can be significantly influenced by gender. Even though women’s entrepreneurship is constantly surging across the world, studies have confirmed that females have comparatively less probability of starting their venture than men (Mwobobia, 2012). There are various reasons that discourage females to enter into an entrepreneurial career, such as fewer opportunities existing for women in places where entrepreneurship is affected by gender-based rules considering entrepreneurship as a men’s job (Verheul et al., 2012). In addition, Bardasi et al. (2011) stated that several institutional and cultural limitations can also hinder the business fortunes in the case of women. Favoritism in the workplace may further

Data were collected fromfinal-yearengineeringstudentsfromtopfiveengineeringinstitutionsacrossNorthernIndia according to National Institute Ranking Framework NIRF List (2021). Purposive sampling was used as it ensures that data were collected from individuals having the same knowledge or experience and participation is deliberate that provides genuine responses (Rajak et al., 2021). A pilot survey among 45 students was conducted to test the questionnaire, and necessary changes wereincorporated into the survey instrument. A structured questionnairevia Google Forms was created and shared with final-year engineering students who had studied any entrepreneurship course as an elective or compulsory subject. Implications of the study 6.1 Theoretical contribution The current study enriches the theoretical knowledge on EE by using the inclusive framework that is grounded on the HCT (Becker, 1964) and TPB (Ajzen, 1991) that have been predominantly used in the entrepreneurial education effectiveness literature. In light of this,

In light of this, the present study examined the impact of two exogenous constructs, i.e. EE and EA, underpinned by the human capital approach of entrepreneurship (Martin et al., 2013; Unger et al., 2011) and the attitudinal factor of the TPB framework (Ajzen, 1991), respectively, on EIs. Secondly, this study adds to the scarce literature, confirming the significance of the human capital dimension of EE in developing nations (Aboobaker, 2020; Ramadani et al., 2022). Thirdly, this study also advances our theoretical understanding of the moderating impact of gender on EE–EI relationship, which has received limited scholarly attention in developing countries, specifically in India (Roy and Das, 2020). 6.2 Practical contribution The study outcomes offer various practical implications for educational establishments, policymakers and the government. The findings reported positive assertion between EE and EI that recommends the further expansion of entrepreneurship-specific subjects

The findings reported positive assertion between EE and EI that recommends the further expansion of entrepreneurship-specific subjects incorporating the appropriate theoretical and practical components that can fully trigger the students’ entrepreneurial drive. This will further equip students with better entrepreneurial comprehension that transcends a positive EA among students. Furthermore, a significant connection between EE, EA and EI suggests the reinforcement of the compulsory infusion of EE in engineering curriculum. The findings contend that EE contributes to creating competent human capital that propels the entrepreneurial settings in the country. India is engulfed by the graduate unemployment, and hence, creating technology startups as the prime vehicle of employment generation is of utmost importance to cater to this persistent employability crisis in the nation. Moreover, the results revealed that gender does not moderate the EE–EI relationship; this recommends that educational programs should be formulated in such a manner that males and females have equal access to entrepreneurial initiatives like entrepreneurial lectures, seminars, workshops, business plans,

Conclusions The present study seeks to achieve two objectives, i.e. firstly, it examines the influence of EE on EA and EI among engineering students in India, and secondly, it explores whether gender moderates EE–EI relationship. The findings articulated the significant influence of EE on EA and EI, whereas gender does not strengthen EE–EI relationship. It is expected that this research will be helpful to policymakers and the government in developing economies to better acknowledge the various determinants that are antecedents to students’ EI. Initiation of Institute scholarships to UG Students of NITJ
Initiation of Institute Scholarships to UG Students of NITJ. We are pleased to announce that from the academic session 2023-24, NIT Jalandhar has initiated scholarship to the UG Students of NITJ. These scholarships will be processed by Dean Academics. The details of the scheme are as below: 1. SCHOLARSHIP FOR THE FIRST YEAR BTECH STUDENTS: The Scholarship will be awarded to the students taking admission at NIT Jalandhar on All India Rank (AIR) in JEE (Main) examination. This fellowship shall be given from the student welfare fund. The following three categories will be eligible for the Scholarship from first year: 1. A student having All India Rank (AIR) in JEE (Main) up to 3000 shall be awarded scholarship of Rs. 50,000/- in the first year of his/her admission. 2. A student having All India Rank (AIR) in JEE (Main) up to 4000 shall be awarded scholarship of Rs. 30,000/- in the first year of his/her admission.

SCHOLARSHIP FOR THE 2nd to 3rd YEAR STUDENTS: Thereafter, a B.Tech. student of each Department who will be the topper in his/her department by securing a CGPA of 9.0 or above without any backlog from the 2nd year onwards will be awarded Rs. 25,000/- per year. DDHCC-2024
The Department of Electronics & Communication Engineering, Dr. B R Ambedkar NIT Jalandhar has been offering B.Tech programme in Electronics & Communication Engineering since 1989, M.Tech programme in Electronics & Communication Engineering (Full-Time) and VLSI Design (Full Time) from year 2007. The Department also offers Ph.D. program in various specializations, such as Biomedical Engineering, VLSI Design and Communication Systems etc. The course curriculum has been designed compatible to the existing and emerging needs of the industry. The Department has established state-of-the-art laboratories for B.Tech, M.Tech and Ph.D. research work. The Department has advanced Biomedical Signal Processing and Telemedicine Laboratory, VLSI Design Laboratory and Communication System Laboratory with sophisticated research equipments. The department has an advanced VLSI lab sponsored by Ministry of Communication and IT under SMDP-II project. In the VLSI lab Cadence, Mentor graphic, Synopsys, Magma, Coware and Xilinx software’s are available for project/research work. The main objective of this course is to provide theoretical and practical knowledge of the recent trends available in the domain of Microwave and Nano-electronics Devices and their modeling applied to VLSI & communication technology. During this program the scientists, academicians and industry persons in their respective areas of expertise will discuss the current scenario on novel semiconductor and passive devices and their applications used in current trends of research. Resource Persons Renowned experts and researchers from premier Institutions (IIT/NITs) and other organizations and industries will deliver expert lectures. The credit system envisages a continuous evaluation of student’s performance, and provides flexibility for academic progress based on individual ability and convenience, subject to the constraint of the minimum requirements for continuation of the academic programme. The students

The students are awarded a letter grade from the prescribed grading system in each course registered by them. For each pass grade, the students accumulate the course credits as earned credits. The academic performance of the students is indicated in terms of the number of credits that he/she earns and the weighted grade point average. A specified minimum number of credits should be acquired on a semester or session basis to qualify for continuation in the academic programme and the award of a degree. The revised curricula of BTech and MTech programmes have been designed to promote inter-disciplinary, multi-disciplinary and trans- disciplinary education and have provisions for choice-based credit system (CBCS). The centre is committed to explore innovative solutions that address the global challenges of sustainable energy production, environmental conservation, and climate change mitigation. At the Centre for Energy and Environment, the mission is to foster interdisciplinary collaboration among researchers, students, and experts from various fields. By combining expertise from engineering, science, policy, and economics, the aim is to drive impactful research and promote the adoption of environmentally friendly and efficient energy technologies. The centre is at the forefront of cutting-edge research in areas such as renewable energy sources, energy storage systems, electric vehicle, sustainable buildings, energy efficiency, and environmental policy analysis. The centre collaborates with industry partners, government agencies, and international organizations to develop solutions that have real-world applications and positive impacts on society. The curriculum integrates theoretical learning with hands-on experiences, encouraging students to engage in research projects, internships, and fieldwork. Distribution systems have evolved to an extent where smart technologies are needed for their smooth operation. Network reconfiguration is one of the functions of distribution automation that improves the performance of the system by altering the structure of the distribution network. In literature, different network reconfiguration problems have been resolved with various methods. However, the active power loss minimization problem is considered most of all, because if these losses are less than the standard, the distribution companies can benefit monetarily. In addition, during the last few decades, distribution system reliability has been developed to provide interruption free electricity services. With improved system reliability, power distribution companies can save the expenses that are spent on a distribution system's maintenance and operation after a power failure.

Its motto ‘Unity and Discipline’ has guided the NCC in its long-standing effort to mould young volunteers into disciplined and responsible citizens of India. Over the years, in response to the evolving environment, the NCC’s initial military orientation was augmented by dimensions of social service and adventure training. The ‘Aim’ of the NCC laid out in 1988 have stood the test of time and continue to meet the requirements expected of it in the current socio–economic scenario of the country. The NCC aims at developing character, comradeship, discipline, a secular

ABOUT THE WORKSHOP Participants will learn about privacy-enabled situational-aware frameworks and their representation using graph databases, graph analytics, and enhanced search algorithms. These techniques ensure data privacy while maintaining situational awareness capabilities. The course will offer participants a comprehensive understanding of graph machine learning structures. They will learn how to analyze social networks, extract valuable information, model human emotions, and gain insights into social relationships using graph-based approaches. Office of the Dean Faculty Welfare Presentation Criteria The presentation (Power Point Presentation) may be planned for 15-20 minutes, but should not exceed 20 minutes under any circumstances. The presentation will consist of two components. Component-I: Should not exceed 5 minutes  Educational qualifications  Research and development activities  Outreach activities  Administrative assignments  Any other achievement Component-II: Should not exceed 10 minutes  The candidate is required to deliver a lecture in the given area of specialization Criteria of Assessment Based on the parameters presented in Component-I and Component-II, the Committee will make assessment regarding the suitability of the candidate for appointment by awarding grades such as ‘A’, ‘B’, ‘C’, ‘D’ and E with ‘A’ representing the most suitable category and ‘E’ the least suitable. The Committee will particularly assess the ‘Teaching Ability’, ‘Research and Development Potential’, ‘Query addressing capability’ and ‘Administrative Capabilities’. The initiative addresses the significant issue of improper agricultural waste management, which contributes to pollution and health problems, especially in regions like Punjab, Haryana, and Delhi NCR. Participants will learn about organic farming techniques, composting, and waste recycling to enhance soil health and productivity without synthetic chemicals. This programme will be organized by the Skill Development Centre at NIT Jalandhar. This program spans five days and includes both theoretical sessions and hands- on practical training. This initiative aims to promote environmental sustainability, generate employment opportunities, and foster entrepreneurship among rural communities. ABOUT THE CENTRE In today's fast-changing world, having a skilled and adaptable workforce is essential. To meet this need and reduce the gap between job seekers' skills and employers' requirements, the Skill Development Centre (SDC) plays a key role. Many job seekers face unemployment or underemployment because they lack the right skills, which affects economic growth and productivity. The SDC addresses this challenge by offering industry-relevant training programs designed to equip individuals with the knowledge and abilities needed to succeed in the job market. These programs help participants gain skills for various sectors, opening up opportunities for employment or entrepreneurship. By empowering India's youth through skill-building, the SDC contributes to creating a more capable and confident workforce, ready to meet the demands of modern industries and build a brighter economic future. Microplastic pollution is a significant environmental concern due to its widespread presence and potential health impacts. Thus, the main objective of this course is to introduce participants to the source, occurrence and estimation of microplastics, and understand various strategies to mitigate its presence from the environment. This STC would benefit faculty, research scholars and students as they update themselves on the recent progress in nanomaterials and their applications. The candidate must have a bachelor’s degree from a recognized institute/university in any stream with 60% marks for Open/OBC-NCL/EWS candidates and 55% for SC/ST/PWD candidates or equivalent CGPA (more than or equal to 6.5 CGPA for Open/OBC-NCL/EWS candidates and 6 CGPA for SC/ST/PWD candidates). ii. BT Biotechnology Section 1: Engineering Mathematics Linear Algebra: Matrices and determinants; Systems of linear equations; Eigen values and Eigen vectors. Calculus: Limits, continuity and differentiability; Partial derivatives, maxima and minima; Sequences and series; Test for convergence. Differential Equations: Linear and nonlinear first order ODEs, higher order ODEs with constant coefficients; Cauchy’s and Euler’s equations; Laplace transforms. Probability and Statistics: Mean, median, mode and standard deviation; Random variables; Poisson, normal and binomial distributions; Correlation and regression analysis. Numerical Methods: Solution of linear and nonlinear algebraic equations; Integration by trapezoidal and Simpson’s rule; Single step method for differential equations. Section 2: General Biology Biochemistry: Biomolecules - structure and function; Biological membranes - structure, membrane channels and pumps, molecular motors, action potential and transport processes; Basic concepts and regulation of metabolism of carbohydrates, lipids, amino acids and nucleic acids; Photosynthesis, respiration and electron transport chain. Enzymes - Classification, catalytic and regulatory strategies; Enzyme kinetics - Michaelis-Menten equation; Enzyme inhibition - competitive, non-competitive and uncompetitive inhibition.

PosterSessionNews
The Department of Mathematics and Computing, NITJ organized an exciting and thought- provoking Poster Presentation Session where the Department's research scholars presented their state-of-the-art work in the diverse range of topics. It was organized as part of the department's ongoing efforts to promote scholarly communication and foster interdisciplinary collaboration. Each presenter shared their innovative research, offering insights into their findings and engaging with attendees through thought-provoking discussions. Attendees had the chance to discuss the latest trends exchange ideas, and form connections that may lead to collaborative projects in the future. The poster presentation session not only served as a platform to showcase the department's ongoing research but also highlighted the department's commitment to nurturing the next generation of mathematicians, computer scientists, and engineers. The head of the Department of Mathematics and Computing, Dr. R. R. Sinha, stated, "We wanted to create an environment where both students and faculty could showcase their work and exchange
title: PosterSessionNews

to create an environment where both students and faculty could showcase their work and exchange ideas." These kinds of gatherings are crucial to creating that feeling of community. Course Instructor Dr Gopal Madabhushi is a Professor of Civil Engineering at the University of Cambridge, UK and the Director of the Schofield Centre. He is also the Head of the Geotechnical and Geo- Environmental Group at Cambridge. His expertise extends from dynamic centrifuge modelling to the time domain finite element analyses of earthquake engineering problems. He has an active interest in the areas of soil liquefaction, soil-structure interaction and liquefaction resistant measures and their performances. He has acted as an expert consultant to the industry on many geotechnical and earthquake engineering problems e.g. Mott MacDonald, Royal Haskonig and Ramboll-Whitby, UK. He has an active interest in post-earthquake reconnaissance work and has led engineering teams from UK to 921 Ji-Ji earthquake of 1999 in Taiwan, the Bhuj earthquake of 2001 in India and many other missions. The load acting on a structure is dependent not only on the environment and location (for example wind, wave, temperature and unknowns related to climate change) but also on unpredictable natural hazards (for example Tsunamis and earthquake and its associated effects such as subsurface liquefaction). In such cases, the soil mass which is surrounding the pile plays a key-role in providing lateral support for the pile. Here comes the necessity of studying the soil- pile interaction. The nature of pile–soil interaction is three dimensional and to complicate the problem further, soil is a nonlinear and anisotropic medium. This course will bring out the assumptions, theories and application methods for modelling soil-pile interaction for various typical field situations. This course is highly specialized and is aimed at faculty members, motivated undergraduate and post graduate students in civil engineering. Practicing civil engineers will also find this course very helpful and refreshing. Course participants will learn these topics through lectures,

Course Objectives • Exposing the participants about the basic concepts behaviour of pile foundations under static loads. • Exposing the participants about the behaviour of single pile & pile group while lateral load acting on it. • To give an idea about the interaction of soil with lateral movement of piles under lateral loading. To identify possible failure mechanisms of piles that can occur under the action of lateral loading. • To provide an exposure to the practical problems with suitable examples through case studies. • To provide a clear knowledge of interaction analysis of single pile and pile group with conventional methods and numerical methods. University)  Prof. Arvind Keprate (University of Oslo, Norway)  Dr. Sumit Sood (University of Lille, France)  Prof. Tej Singh (Savaria Institute of Technology, Hungary)  Dr. Prampreet Singh (IIT Bombay) Online One Week Short Term Course on Design and Optimization of Thermal Systems: An Experimental and Computational Approach June 16–20, 2025 Department of Mechanical Engineering Dr B R Ambedkar National Institute of Technology Jalandhar Jalandhar, Punjab – 144008 INTRODUCTION Computational science and Machine learning (ML) and computational science have revolutionized the way that complicated engineering problems are solved, especially when it comes to thermal system design and optimization. The interaction of thermodynamics, fluid dynamics, and heat transfer makes thermal systems—which include applications like heat exchangers, HVAC systems, renewable energy systems, and thermal management in electronics—inherently complex. Innovative strategies that integrate machine- learning techniques for optimization, prediction, and decision-making with computational tools for modelling and simulation are needed to address these issues. With a focus on thermal systems, an experimental shortterm course in computational
title: STC DOTS

text:

and decision-making with computational tools for modelling and simulation are needed to address these issues. With a focus on thermal systems, an experimental shortterm course in computational and machine learning equips participants with the skills and information necessary to successfully address these issues, with a particular emphasis on design and optimization.  OBJECTIVE OF THE COURSE  This course aims to close the gap between computer science, machine learning, and thermal engineering. For five days, attendees will study how thermal   systems may be modeled and simulated using computational techniques, and how machine learning can improve these models by anticipating system behavior, optimizing performance, and offering data-driven insights. The course's experimental design fosters creativity and innovation by encouraging participants to apply what they have learned to actual thermal system problems. At the nexus of thermal systems, machine learning, and computational science, this experimental short-term course provides an engaging and dynamic learning environment. Providing a hands-on, practical learning experience, this course empowers them to promote

Providing a hands-on, practical learning experience, this course empowers them to promote efficiency and creativity in the design, analysis, and optimization of thermal systems. With an emphasis on both machine learning and computational approaches, this course equips students with state-of-the-art tools and methods to address the difficulties of contemporary thermal engineering. COURSE CONTENT  Day 01:16.06.2025 Morning: Fundamentals on design and optimization of thermal systems Evening: Hands-on Training: - CFD Analysis and optimization of Single and Multiphase Flow & heat Transfer systems  Day 02:17.06.2025 Morning: AI/MI of integrated thermal technologies Evening: Hands-on Training: CFD Analysis and optimization of Single and Multiphase Flow & heat Transfer problems (Ansys-Fluent)  Day 03:18.06.2025 Morning: Fundamentals of CFD in Microchannels (Single and Multiphase flow) Evening: Hands on Training: MATLAB solution of diffusion and advection (convection) problems.  Day 4:19.06.2025 Morning: Design and optimization of solar thermal systems Evening: Hands on training: - CFD results validation

Online Self-sponsored 5 day workshop on "Molecular Dynamics Simulation & Analysis" Organized by Department of Mechanical Engineering Dr. B. R. Ambedkar National Institute of Technology Jalandhar-144008 Punjab www.nitj.ac.in Course Coordinators Dr. Sumit Sharma & Dr. Ashok Kumar Assistant Professor, Department of Mechanical Engineering NIT-Jalandhar Ph no.: 8146871758,6239939218 E-mail: sharmas@nitj.ac.in, baghaak@nitj.ac.in Molecular modelling and simulation involve developing representations of physical systems at atomistic/molecular-level detail, and using such models to simulate (or mimic) physical processes/phenomena on a computer for studying properties of interest. Molecular simulations can also be used to calculate or predict properties and quantities that may be difficult to observe experimentally. The workshop will introduce the field of molecular modelling and simulation to the participants through lectures, demonstrations, and hands-on sessions, in online mode. In particular, the focus will be on the classical molecular dynamics (MD) simulation technique. The simulations will be conducted and demonstrated using Materials Studio and the open-source software package LAMMPS. The software packages VMD and OVITO (also open source) will be used to
title: brochure mdsa 2025

brochure mdsa 2025
simulations will be conducted and demonstrated using Materials Studio and the open-source software package LAMMPS. The software packages VMD and OVITO (also open source) will be used to visualize molecular models and simulation results. This workshop aims to review various molecular simulation techniques with a focus on how practical industrial problems can be solved using molecular simulations by helping screen a range of potential raw materials without the need to actually synthesise such products/chemicals. Such simulation techniques may reduce the huge amount of money spent on chemicals and human resources, for synthesizing specific products. The workshop shall involve experts working in the area of molecular simulations who are engaged in using such techniques for developing their own codes or are using similar software to understand and solve fundamental and practical problems related to Mechanical Engineering. The Institute Dr B R Ambedkar National Institute of Technology (NIT), Jalandhar was established in the year 1986 as Regional Engineering College and was given the status of National Institute of Technology (Deemed University) by the Government of India on 17 October 2002 under the aegis of Ministry of Human Resource Development, New Delhi. The Ministry of Human Resource Development, Government of India has declared the Institute as 'Institute of National Importance' under the act of Parliament-2007. The Institute offers Bachelor of Technology (BTech), Master of Technology (MTech), Master of Science (MSc), Master of Business Administration (MBA) and Doctor of Philosophy (PhD) programs in several disciplines of Engineering, Science & Technology and Management. The Department The Department of Civil Engineering offers B.Tech. in the discipline of Civil Engineering ever since its inception in the year 1989. The department has been offering M.Tech. Programme in Structural & Construction Engineering since 2004 and Geotechnical & Geo-environmental Engineering since 2017. The doctoral programmes in different specializations were started in the year 2006. The

The Department has also been selected as ‘DST-FIST Sponsored Department’ by the Ministry of Science and Technology, Government of India. The Department has established state-of-the art laboratories with sophisticated equipment for undergraduate courses and research work. Overview of the Course This course is designed to provide an in-depth understanding of the importance and necessity of improving ground and soil conditions for various construction and maintenance of transportation infrastructure. The course provides an overview of ground improvement techniques, emphasizing mechanical stabilization, hydraulic modification, and soil stabilization using admixtures. It covers soil modification by inclusion and confinement, including both shallow and deep compaction methods. The properties of compacted soil and compaction control are examined, with specific focus on deep compaction techniques such as dynamic compaction, vibro- compaction, and the vibro-float technique, along with controlled blasting. Participants will learn about subsurface investigation methods
title: GIAN 2700177

text:

compaction, and the vibro-float technique, along with controlled blasting. Participants will learn about subsurface investigation methods for infrastructure projects, encompassing both laboratory and in-situ test methods. The course addresses ground improvement by drainage, exploring dewatering methods and the consolidation of soft soils. Foundation treatment methods for soft soils, including surcharge preloading, vertical drains, sand drains, wick drains, or prefabricated vertical drains, and vacuum consolidation, are detailed. The course offers a comprehensive exploration of grouting techniques, discussing various types of grouting methods, strategies for grouting under challenging conditions, and the intricacies of soil anchoring. This includes a detailed examination of the types and design considerations for soil anchoring and soil nailing. Additionally, the course addresses the stabilization of organic and peat soils, providing insights into the unique challenges and solutions associated with these soil types. Mechanically stabilized reinforced retaining walls are another key focus, with an in-depth look at the various types of geosynthetics used in their construction and the principles of designing retaining walls with

This short-term course on "Practical Approaches to Soil Improvement and Sustainable Geotechnical Solutions" is designed to provide participants with a comprehensive understanding of various ground improvement methods used in the construction and maintenance of transportation infrastructure. Objectives The primary objectives of the course are as follows: • Understand the critical need for ground and soil improvement in infrastructure projects, recognizing how various techniques can enhance soil properties and support structural stability. • Explore comprehensive knowledge of different ground improvement methods, including mechanical stabilization, hydraulic modification, and soil stabilization using admixtures and non-traditional stabilizers like geopolymers. • Learn techniques for both shallow and deep soil compaction, including dynamic compaction, vibro-compaction, and the use of vertical drains, ensuring they can control and enhance soil properties effectively. • Analyze various soil stabilization methods involving cement, lime, and industrial waste, understanding the chemical reactions
title: GIAN 2700177

About the Short Term Course In today's data-driven textile industry, understanding and applying statistical techniques and experimental design is essential for achieving quality excellence, innovation, and process optimization. This Short Term Course (STC) is designed to provide textile students, researchers, and professionals with practical knowledge and skills in statistics and Design of Experiments (DoE), tailored specifically for textile applications. Participants will learn to plan experiments, analyze data, and make data-driven decisions in various textile processes. Contents / Topics of STC  Basic Statistic  ANOVA and Regression  Inferential Statistics  Design of Experiments  Process Capability  Advanced DoE Techniques  Data and Subjective Rank  Project & Case Studies  Acceptance Sampling and Statistic for Descriptive Data  Software Tools in Textile Data Analysis Instructions for Registration

ABOUT NIT JALANDHAR Dr B R Ambedkar National Institute of Technology Jalandhar is amongst the 31 NITs established by the Ministry of HRD, Government of India. The institute came into existence in the year 1988 (earlier Regional Engineering College Jalandhar) and obtained the status “Institute of National Importance” by Act of Parliament 2007 under the NIT Act 2007 amended as NITSER Act 2012. The institute is offering B Tech programmes in various disciplines like Computer Science and Engineering, Electronics and Communication Engineering, Information Technology, Instrumentation and Control Engineering, Mechanical Engineering, Civil Engineering, Textile Technology, Biotechnology, and Industrial & Production Engineering. In addition to B.Tech programmes, the institute offers M.Sc. programmes in Physics, Chemistry, and Mathematics, M.Tech programmes in all Engineering departments, and Ph.D. programmes. ABOUT SPARC The Scheme for Promotion of Academic and Research Collaboration (SPARC), launched by the Ministry of Human Resource Development, Government of India, is designed to enhance the research ecosystem of India's higher educational institutions. SPARC facilitates academic and research partnerships between top Indian

Human Resource Development, Government of India, is designed to enhance the research ecosystem of India's higher educational institutions. SPARC facilitates academic and research partnerships between top Indian institutions and leading global institutions through joint research projects that include mobility for students and faculty. This initiative aims to bring world-class expertise to address critical national challenges, expose Indian scholars to top international collaborators, offer extended stays for international faculty in India, provide Indian students with opportunities to work in leading laboratories, strengthen bilateral research relationships, and improve the international rankings of Indian institutions. ABOUT THE WORKSHOP This one-week intensive workshop focuses on the development and application of Next-Gen AI Frameworks for Real-Time Flash Flood Risk Management in Mountainous Terrains. Aimed at faculty members, research scholars, and industry professionals, the program will explore how Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) are transforming hydrological modeling by enabling real-time analysis of complex environmental datasets. Special emphasis will be placed on cloud-based architectures that support scalable and rapid flood risk

Learning (ML) are transforming hydrological modeling by enabling real-time analysis of complex environmental datasets. Special emphasis will be placed on cloud-based architectures that support scalable and rapid flood risk analytics, essential for early warning systems in steep and vulnerable terrains like the Himalayas. Participants will learn how deep learning techniques can be applied to accurately forecast flash floods in mountainous regions, where traditional models often fall short due to data limitations and complex topography. The workshop will also highlight the importance of uncertainty quantification in AI-based predictions, ensuring that model outputs are robust and actionable for risk assessment. Discussions will include the impacts of climate change on flood behavior, with strategies to integrate long-term environmental shifts into real-time forecasting frameworks. Through regional case studies and real-world examples, the workshop will provide a practical perspective on the challenges and solutions involved in deploying AI systems in mountain catchments. with the support of Department of Science and Technology for enhancing the startup ecosystem. The vision of TBI is to make startup and innovation part of NITJ system by offering service such as Pre-Incubation, Incubation, Mentorship, and Virtual Incubation. In 2023, the startup India fund recognized these activities of NITJ TBI and awarded grant of 5.25 crores. This grant is a testament to the efforts of TBI. Through this grant, seed fund has been given to startups such as RFvis Technologies, Lifetronics Engineering and RAMCOM. Currently, there are 17 startups registered in TBI which are working in the domain of healthcare, edutech, software services, security, ecommerce etc. The TBI offers complete infrastructure and guidance facilities. These facilities are available to - Faculty/Staff of the NITJ (Current and Retired); Students, research scholars and current project staff of NITJ, Alumni of NITJ, Universities/Institutions having R&D collaboration with NITJ, and others people who want to startup. 4.4 ISRO funded Space-Technology Incubation Centre

In the modern digital landscape, the rapid growth of data has necessitated the development of scalable techniques to analyze and extract insights from vast datasets. As the volume, velocity, and variety of data continue to expand, traditional methods of analysis prove inadequate. Scalable approaches involve employing advanced techniques, algorithms, and technologies to handle massive datasets without compromising on performance or accuracy. This will enable organizations to extract valuable information from Data Mountains, paving the way for informed decision-making and innovation. Cutting-edge graph mining involves the application of advanced techniques to analyze intricate relationships within complex networks or graphs. Cutting-edge techniques employ algorithms that reverse these structures to uncover patterns, clusters, influential nodes, and insights, enabling a deeper understanding of interconnected data. This course will serve as a comprehensive guide, unraveling the intricacies of scalable data analysis while delving into the forefront of graph mining innovations. text:
DE GE Notice
Guidelines for DE/GE Students have to complete 08 electives towards completion of B.Tech. Programme, with following requirements: Out of 08 Electives- • At least 04 DE (from respective department) • At least 02 GE (DE offered by all other Engineering/Sciences/Management departments) • Remaining 02 electives to be opted from DE/GE. A student is also allowed to pursue a maximum of 02 generic elective courses in online mode through Massive Open Online Courses (MOOC) platforms like NPTEL, Swayam, and other similar reputed platforms provided the same courses are not being offered in the institute. The student will have the option to pick these courses from Engineering, Sciences, Management, Humanities, History, Music, Art, Philosophy, Finance, Psychology etc., However, prior approval from respective DUGC is required for all such courses. The courses to be opted through MOOC platforms should meet either of the following criteria: • Credits – Minimum 3 credits • Duration – Minimum 8 weeks • Contact hours – Minimum 32 hrs
title: DE GE Notice

text:
DE GE Notice
criteria: • Credits – Minimum 3 credits • Duration – Minimum 8 weeks • Contact hours – Minimum 32 hrs The result of the candidate in respective online course would be mapped to an appropriate letter grade as per the norms of the institute. Further, the letter grade awarded by the respective MOOCS course will be considered as such. Absolute marks/percentage will be converted into appropriate letter grade using absolute grading criterion if letter grade not awarded by the respective MOOCs courses. Further, the students who will pursue GE in online mode through MOOCs platform will be required to obtain a Pass Certificate for that particular course from the concerned MOOCs platform. The credits earned through online courses will be counted towards major degree. However, students pursuing 6-months internship during their 7th semester/8th semester have to complete 05 electives towards completion of B.Tech. programme, with following requirements: Out of 05 Electives- • 03 DE (from respective department) • 02 GE (DE offered by all other Engineering/Sciences/Management departments)

Press Note on short term course (STC) on Characterisation of Polymers & Textiles Department of Textile Technology, Dr. B. R. Ambedkar, National Institute of Technology Jalandhar, Punjab is organized a five day short term course (STC) on “Characterisation of Polymers & Textiles” from July 25 to 29, 2025” in virtual mode. The organizing team of STC comprised of Dr. Vinay Midha, Dr. Lalit Jajpura, Dr. Palaniswamy N. K., Dr. Mukesh Bajya, and Dr. Anilkumar Yadav. The STC assembled a diverse group of esteemed speakers such as Prof. Ashwini Agrawal, Prof. Bhanu Nandan, Prof. Leena Nebhani from IIT Delhi; Prof. A. Mukhopadhyay and Prof. A. Chatterjee from NIT Jalandhar, and leading technology firms such as Thermo Fisher Scientific, Bruker India, Anton Paar, Malvern Panalytical, and Mettler-Toledo delivered insightful sessions. The course covered essential areas like thermal analysis, nanocomposite development, surface characterisation, geotextiles, colour analysis, and contact angle/tensiometer applications. About the Short-Term Course This five-day online short-term course on Modeling and Identification of Physiological Systems provides a comprehensive blend of theory, computation, and application. It begins with an introduction to mathematical modeling approaches used to represent key physiological systems, such as the cardiovascular, respiratory, and nervous systems, and progresses to methods for estimating model parameters and states. Participants will learn techniques for processing physiological signals like ECG and EEG, and apply both physics-based and data-driven modeling

Participants will learn techniques for processing physiological signals like ECG and EEG, and apply both physics-based and data-driven modeling paradigms. Furthermore, this STC explores applications of control theory to physiological control systems, highlighting how feedback and regulation mechanisms are modelled and analysed in a biomedical context. It also examines the role of machine learning and deep learning in classifying physiological conditions using real-world datasets. Participants will gain exposure to uncertainty quantification, explainability in AI models, and current clinical applications. The course will encourage participants to apply their learning to real-world problems, encouraging practical thinking and clear model understanding. This course is ideal for researchers, engineers, and healthcare professionals interested in computational physiology and biomedical data science. Dr B R Ambedkar National Institute of Technology Jalandhar, Punjab, India Department of Computer Science & Engineering Self Sponsored Online Short Term Course on AI-Powered Innovation: Integrating Future-Ready Technologies in Real-World Applications (November 05-09, 2025) ABOUT THE ONLINE STC The online STC provides a comprehensive overview of AI- powered innovation and the integration of future-ready technologies into real-world applications. It introduces the fundamentals of artificial intelligence, machine learning, and deep learning, and explains their relevance across sectors such as healthcare, finance, education, and manufacturing. The program explores advanced topics like intelligent automation, data-driven decision-making, and predictive analytics. From a networking perspective, the STC delves into the role of AI in next-generation networks, including 5G/6G, highlighting applications such as dynamic resource allocation and real-time anomaly detection. The STC also discusses the privacy challenges associated with AI deployment. Additionally, it provides insights into current research trends, tools, and frameworks supporting AI integration. Overall, the STC offers a well-rounded perspective on harnessing AI for practical innovation and resilient technology development. ABOUT THE DEPARTMENT

Conceptual Understanding A carpentry shop is a workshop where wood and wood-based materials are measured, cut, shaped, and assembled to create structures, furniture, or functional wooden products. The primary function of a carpentry shop is to transform raw timber into usable components or finished items using hand tools, power tools, and machines. Common operations include measuring, marking, cutting, planning, chiseling, drilling, joining, sanding, and finishing. Precision and craftsmanship are critical, as the quality and fit of wooden joints and surfaces directly affect the strength, functionality,

Key elements include careful measurement and marking, cutting, chiseling, planning, and joining, with emphasis on safety, precision, and craftsmanship. A Cross Lap Joint involves two wooden pieces intersecting each other at midpoints, where half of the thickness of each piece is removed so they fit together flush. This joint is commonly used in frameworks, furniture, and structural woodwork where components cross each other. Just like in mechanical fitting (metal work), carpentry also involves precision through operations such as measuring, marking, cutting, chiseling, and finishing, typically performed on a wooden workbench. Accuracy in marking and uniform depth cutting are crucial to ensure a tight and clean fit of the two members. Applications of cross lap joint: Cross lap joints are commonly used in furniture making, timber frameworks, and wooden support structures, such as racks, partitions, and frames. They provide strength and stability at intersecting points. Fig.1 Geometry of a cross lap joint. 2. Tools, Equipment & Materials S. No. Tool / Equipment / Material

Theory Covered in Demonstration for Arc Welding Principle: Arc welding is based on the principle of producing intense heat by creating an electric arc between an electrode and the work piece. The arc melts the base metal and the filler metal (if used), allowing them to fuse upon cooling to form a strong joint. The process relies on a continuous supply of electrical energy to sustain the arc. Figure 1 showcases the electric arc welding set-up and shielded metal arc welding. Working: 1. Power Supply Connection: The welding machine provides either Alternating Current (AC) or Direct Current (DC) to the electrode and workpiece.

Arc Formation: When the electrode tip is brought close to the workpiece, an electric arc is struck, generating temperatures between 3,000–6,000 °C. 3. Metal Fusion: The intense heat melts the base metal and the electrode tip, allowing them to mix and form the weld pool. 4. Protection: Flux coating on the electrode melts to form a gaseous shield and a layer of slag, preventing oxidation and contamination. 5. Cooling: Once the arc is broken, the molten pool solidifies to produce the welded joint. Conceptual Understanding Blacksmithing or Forging is one of the oldest methods used to shape metal, mainly for making small items where exact size is not very important. In this process, the blacksmith heats the metal in an open fire and then shapes it by hitting it with a hammer. Forging means shaping metal by applying pressure (using tools like hammers or presses) while the metal is hot and soft. This usually happens at a high temperature, around 980°C, when the metal becomes easy to bend and
title: Lab Manual Smithy Shop

text:
Lab Manual Smithy Shop
is hot and soft. This usually happens at a high temperature, around 980°C, when the metal becomes easy to bend and form. The place where this work is done is called a smithy or blacksmith’s shop. Hand forging, also called blacksmith work, is a manual process used to make small items. The metal is heated and shaped using hammers and other hand tools. Sometimes machines like power hammers are used to help with the work. Applications of Forging: Forging is used to shape a wide range of metals and alloys, including carbon steels, wrought iron, copper, aluminium, and magnesium alloys. High-performance materials like stainless steel, nickel-based super alloys, and titanium are forged for critical applications, especially in the aerospace industry. 2. 1. Drawing-down: Drawing is the process of stretching the stock while reducing its cross-section locally. Forging the tapered end of a cold is an example of drawing operation. 2. Upsetting: It is the process of increasing the thickness of a metal piece by reducing its length. Only the part to be upset is heated, then hammered at the end—either by hand for small jobs or with a sledgehammer for larger ones. 3. Fullering: Fullers are tools used to narrow metal, helping start the drawing process. They come in two parts and fit into the anvil, with size based on the edge width. 4. Flattering: Flatters are the tools that are made with a perfectly flat face of about 7.5 cm square. These are used for finishing flat surfaces. A flatter of small size is known as set-hammer and is used for finishing near corners and in confined spaces. 5. Swaging: Swages like fullers are also made of high carbon steel and are made in two parts called the top and
title: Lab Manual Smithy Shop

confined spaces. 5. Swaging: Swages like fullers are also made of high carbon steel and are made in two parts called the top and swages. These are used to reduce and finish to round, square or hexagonal forms. For this, the swages are made with half grooves of dimensions to suit the work. 6. Bending: Bending of bars, flats, etc., is done to produce different types of bent shapes such as angles, ovals, circles etc. Sharp bends as well as round bends may be made on the anvil, by choosing the appropriate place on it for the purpose. 7. Cutting (Hot and Cold Chisels): Chisels cut metal in hot or cold states. Cold chisels are long with handles, while hot chisels have slender edges for cutting hot metal. Safety Guideline of Smithy Shop: -  Always hold hot work downward and close to the ground when moving it to avoid burns from accidental collisions.  Use the correct size and type of tongs to grip the work securely and prevent it from bouncing during hammering.  Use only the minimum hammer force needed, striking squarely with the flat face to avoid bruising the metal.  Wear a water face shield and gloves when hammering or handling hot metal.  Always wear steel-toed shoes for foot protection.  Ensure hammer handles are tight and properly wedged to prevent accidents. A hem joint is a folded edge of sheet metal (shown in figure 1), used to:  Remove sharp edges for safety.  Reinforce the edge to prevent deformation.  Improve appearance and durability. Single Hem Joint Definition: In a single hem, the sheet metal edge is folded once (typically 180°) over itself. It is commonly used in ducting, enclosures, automotive panels, and household appliances. Applications of Hem Joint:  Automotive body panels  Ductwork and ventilation systems 

Applications of Hem Joint:  Automotive body panels  Ductwork and ventilation systems  Sheet metal enclosures and boxes  Edge strengthening in furniture and cabinets Purpose of Hemming 1. Reinforcement – Hemming strengthens the sheet metal edge, making it more resistant to bending, cracking, or fracturing under load. 2. Edge Finishing – It provides a smooth, rounded edge, removing sharp or rough edges that could cause injury or reduce product quality. 3. Joining – Hemming can also serve as a joining method by folding the edge of one sheet over another, creating a mechanical interlock. Types of Hems  Closed Hem – The folded edge is completely flattened against the sheet, forming a smooth and flush surface. Common in enclosures and boxes.  Open Hem – The folded edge leaves a small gap or air pocket, not fully flattened. This type is used where flexibility or clearance is required. 

Heel: It is the intersection of the flan and the base of the tool. It is a curved portion at the bottom of the tool. 5. Nose: It is the point where the side cutting edge and end cutting edge intersects. 6. Cutting edge: It is the edge on the face of the tool which removes the material from the workpiece. Conceptual Understanding A foundry shop is a place where metal casting is done. In simple terms, it's a workshop where metal is melted and poured into molds to form desired shapes. The process usually involves making a pattern, preparing a mold (often from sand), melting metal, pouring it into the mold, and letting it cool and solidify. Once solid, the casting is cleaned and finished. Foundries are essential in manufacturing for creating parts used in machines, tools, vehicles, and more.

Basic Terms used in Foundry Mold/Mould: It is a cavity so prepared that can be used to make castings by pouring molten material into it. Pattern: It is a model of any component which is used to prepare molds by placing it in sand. Casting: The molten metal poured into mold, on cooling is known as casting. Cope is the upper part and Drag is the lower part of the molding box. Runner is the passage through which molten metal is poured. Gate is the small passage connecting the runner to the mold cavity. Riser is the passage through which the molten metal rises up after filling the mold cavity.
title: Lab Manual Foundary Shop

text:

Gate is the small passage connecting the runner to the mold cavity. Riser is the passage through which the molten metal rises up after filling the mold cavity. Pouring Basin is the enlarged portion in the form of a countersunk, at the top of the runner. Core is a body of sand which is used to form a cavity of desired shape and size in a casting. Working/Key Operations in a Foundry Shop: 1. Pattern Making – Creating a replica of the desired casting to form the mold cavity. 2. Mold Preparation – Making the mold around the pattern using materials like sand or metal. 3. Core Making – Producing cores to create internal cavities or complex shapes within the casting. 4. Melting – Heating metal until it becomes molten and ready for pouring. 5. Pouring – Pouring the molten metal into the prepared mold cavity. 6. Cooling and Solidification – Allowing the molten metal to cool and solidify into the mold shape.

Shakeout – Removing the solidified casting from the mold. 8. Cleaning – Removing residual sand, scale, and excess metal (like gates and risers) from the casting. 9. Inspection and Finishing – Checking the casting for defects and performing any necessary machining or surface finishing. 4. Theory In this experiment, a mold is prepared using green sand and a single-piece solid pattern. Green sand, a mixture of silica sand, clay, and water, is packed around the pattern to form the mold cavity. A solid pattern is a one-piece replica of the final casting (Step Pulley, as shown in figure 1), commonly used for simple shapes without intricate cores. It is durable, easy to handle, and ideal for low to medium volume production. The pattern is placed in the drag flask, and sand is compacted using a hand rammer. After leveling and venting, the pattern is carefully removed, leaving an impression that forms the mold. The cut section schematic of the process is shown in figure 2.

Taps are used to cut internal threads (female threads, like in a nut) in a pre-drilled hole, while dies are used to cut external threads (male threads, like on a bolt or screw) on a rod or bolt. This process allows for the secure fastening of parts using screws, bolts, and nuts. Elaboration:  Taps: Taps are cutting tools used to create internal threads within a hole. They have a series of cutting edges that gradually remove material as the tap is rotated, forming the helical thread profile. 

They also have cutting edges that remove material to form the desired thread profile when rotated around the workpiece.  Applications: Tapping and dieing are essential for various tasks, including:  Creating new threads: When a new threaded hole or bolt is needed.  Repairing damaged threads: Restoring damaged threads on existing components.  Ensuring proper fit: Ensuring threads are accurate and compatible for proper assembly.  Techniques: Several techniques are important for successful tapping and dieing, including:  Proper lubrication: Using cutting fluid to reduce friction, heat, and chip build-up.  Maintaining alignment: Ensuring the tap or die is perpendicular to the workpiece to create straight threads.  Chip breaking: Periodically backing out the tap or die to break off and remove chips, preventing them from jamming.  Types of Taps: Different tap types exist for various applications, such as:

Theory The experiment to control a lamp from three different switches demonstrates the concept of intermediate (multi-way) switching, commonly used in staircases, corridors, or large rooms where a lamp needs to be operated from more than two locations. This setup involves the use of 2 two-way (SPDT) switches and one intermediate (four-way) switch placed between them. The intermediate switch has four terminals and allows current to be redirected based on its position, enabling control of the lamp from a third point. The circuit works by forming different paths for the current to either complete or break the circuit, thus turning the lamp ON or OFF from any of the three switches. Figure 1 shows the circuit diagram for connections. This wiring method is a practical application of switching principles in household and commercial electrical installations.

ABOUT THE SHORT-TERM COURSE The importance of power electronics has grown over the years due to several factors. Power electronics is interdisciplinary in nature, and it is used in a wide variety of applications like electric drives, power quality in power systems and renewable energy systems, etc... OBJECTIVES OF THE COURSE The objective of this one-week Short-Term Course is to provide participants with a comprehensive understanding of research methodology and to develop essential research skills. Specifically, the course seeks to:  Introduce participants to the fundamental principles, types, and significance of research in academic and professional contexts.  Enable participants to identify and formulate research problems, objectives, and hypotheses systematically.  Familiarize them with appropriate research designs, sampling methods, and tools for data collection.  Develop competence in data analysis and interpretation using basic statistical techniques.  Promote awareness of research ethics, plagiarism prevention, and proper referencing styles.  Equip participants with the ability to prepare well-structured research proposals, reports, and papers. This program is designed to build a strong foundation in research methodology and inspire participants to undertake high-quality, impactful research in their respective fields. COURSE CONTENTS The important contents of the short term course are as follows:  Introduction to Research, Research Design, Data collection, Sample design, Sampling Techniques.

International Conference Chemical Constellation Cheminar (C3) – 2026 Next Generation Materials for Energy and Environment (Hybrid Mode) April 03-04, 2026 Organized by Department of Chemistry Dr B R Ambedkar National Institute of Technology Jalandhar, Punjab, India About Conference The aim of the conference C3-2026 is to create a platform for the faculty, researchers, students and industrial experts for exchanging the latest research advancements in materials and interdisciplinary areas towards the sustainable technological development. During the conference, the participants will have an opportunity to interact with the researchers from the various parts of the world. Participants will also have the opportunities to establish the research collaborations with the industries and academia through different interactive sessions. Over the course of two days, participants and experts will present their latest findings and the future perspectives in development of materials for applications in environment, healthcare, energy, electronics, sensors, textiles, defence, and other related areas. I Grade Notice Extension
End-semester examination because of extraordinary emergency situation. 75% attendance in a course is necessary for being eligible for request of ‘I’ grade in that course. An application requesting an ‘I’ grade should be made at the earliest, but not later than two days after the End-semester examinations to the concerned Head of department through the concerned course coordinator. Depending on the merits of the case in discussions with concerned course coordinator, HoD will recommend allotment of ‘I’ grade. An ‘I’ grade must be converted by the course coordinator into an appropriate letter grade after conducting the examination. The examination can be conducted any time after the allotment of ‘I’ grade but within 15 days of the start of classes of the following Even/Odd semester, failing which it will be converted to U grade. Note: All ‘I” Grade Examination and Results will be completed by 03.02.2026 after which the ‘I’ Grade will be converted to ‘U’ Grade by the Examination Section.

Supplementary Examination Notice January 2026
1. A student obtaining 'U' grade in a theory course may register for a supplementary exam in that course. However, the supplementary exam will not be available for Laboratory Courses. 2. The maximum number of times a supplementary examination can be taken for each course is 02. If the student fails to clear the course in 02 supplementary chances, he/she will have to repeat the course as an additional course with U grade. 3. The candidates during supplementary exam shall be awarded one grade less than the actual grade obtained and the highest grade that a student can get through the Supplementary Exam shall be ‘D’. Emergency Preparedness
Emergency preparedness involves health-related incidents. To learn how to implement plans and actions effectively for wellbeing of mass health care. Preparedness involves training, mock drills, staying calm, assessing the situation for safety, calling for emergency services, administering appropriate first aid, providing comfort, and communicating with responders. Developing a trained response team which includes training to trained students and develop a skilled response team capable of handling such situations. Recognizing when to call for professional medical help, Safe handling and transportation of injured persons. On specific instructions from their BoGs, the Institute has sought clarification on including same in their ensuing advertisements for faculty recruitments and its applicability on serving faculty members. , 3. 3. In this regard, attention is drawn towards Note 1 (1) of the Statutes which states that “any change in the grade pay will be through open advertisement and on recommendations’ of duly selection committee, except where specifically exempted in these rules”: Thus there is no provision ‘of promotion in NITs as per the Act and statutes and open recruitment at each stage,~ combined with Four-Tier Flexible Faculty Cadre Structure is the {un yae0AN Py Sey Hate an “AY - 46 - cornerstone of these Institutions of National Importance to recruit and retain only the best of the best teaching talent. In flexi cadre, a faculty appointed at any level and moving forward in next level carries his own position, as his selection to higher grade won’t change the actual numbers of faculty in position. 4. Note 1 (5) of the Statutes states that “for the department which are not having any vacancy, movement in higher academic grade pay or cadre shall be
title: Annexure-II a Gazette Notification 2017

text:
